outcomes.note: Confirmed by executing the rule on the reviewer's fixture: on `x = {1, 2` followed by a line `|> IO.inspect()`, the rule emitted `x = {1, 2\n    |> IO.inspect()}` (the tuple `{1, IO.inspect(2)}`), and a second executed check showed the alternative placement `x = {1, 2}\n|> IO.inspect()` also parses with a different AST — so the rule was silently choosing one of two valid meanings, while its own moduledoc promised to stay silent rather than pick a placement. Pinned with two tests that fail on the old code for exactly this reason: a fix test asserting the operator-continuation source is returned byte-for-byte untouched, and an analyze test asserting no issue is reported (the rule never flags what it will not fix). Fixed by adding a fourth guard, `sole_placement/3`: after a repair candidate is found, the rule tries appending the `}` to each earlier non-blank line of the literal, and refuses the whole repair if any of those also makes the source parse. Lines ending in `,` are excluded as competing placements, by the same reasoning as the existing dangling-comma guard (closing after a trailing comma silently drops an element, so the comma pins the next line inside the literal) — this is what keeps every previously-admitted fixture repaired byte-for-byte identically. The moduledoc now documents the new guard ("Four guards" with a worked `|>` example). Proven: the full rule battery passes (33 tests), the fast gate is green (mix format, mix compile --warnings-as-errors, mix test --exclude corpus --exclude idempotency: 9024 tests, 0 failures), and re-running the original reproduction shows the rule now leaves the ambiguous source untouched. Committed as 38c0d19 (rule + both test files).
